subject: physics
scope: PD-26/27/28 fast packed explainer: one board (one resistor, its meter unknown until the calculation); voltage, current and resistance defined in plain words with their units; Ohm's law in plain words and in NCERT 12.3's words with its condition (same temperature); V = I R and both rearrangements; three cases on the same board (2 V -> 0.20 A, 4 V -> 0.40 A, 20 ohm at 2 V -> 0.10 A); the V-I straight line through the origin with slope R; the hot filament as the bounded qualitative exception

sources.title: NCERT Class 10 Science
sources.section: Chapter 12 'Electricity', section 12.3 'Ohm's Law' (statement: V ∝ I provided the temperature remains the same; V/I = R; V = IR; Activity 12.1 and the V–I graph for a nichrome wire, a straight line through the origin; 1 ohm = 1 volt / 1 ampere)

sources.title: NCERT Class 10 Science
sources.section: Chapter 'Electricity', section 12.1 'Electric Current and Circuit' (I = Q/t, the net charge flowing through a cross-section per unit time; 1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second; the ammeter measures current, in series)

sources.title: NCERT Class 10 Science
sources.section: Chapter 'Electricity', section 12.2 'Electric Potential and Potential Difference' (V = W/Q, work done per unit charge; 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb)

sources.title: NCERT Class 10 Science
sources.section: Chapter 'Electricity', section 'Heating Effect of Electric Current' (the electric bulb filament gets very hot)

nodes.statement: Say what voltage, current and resistance are, with their units; state Ohm's law in plain words and recognise NCERT 12.3's statement with its condition (same temperature); use V = I R, I = V/R and R = V/I on three cases (2 V, 10 Ω → 0.20 A; 4 V → 0.40 A; 2 V, 20 Ω → 0.10 A); read the V–I graph as a straight line through the origin whose slope is R; know that a hot filament bends the line.
Electric current is the charge passing a point (a cross-section of the wire) each second; its unit is the ampere (A), one coulomb per second; the ammeter in series reads it.
nodes.plain_words: The meter counts the charge passing each second: the current, in amps.

nodes.statement: Resistance is the property of a conductor to oppose (hold back) the flow of charge through it; it is the constant ratio V/I at constant temperature, measured in ohms (Ω).
nodes.plain_words: The resistor holds the flow back: resistance, ten ohms.

nodes.statement: The potential difference (voltage) between two points is the work done (energy given) per unit charge moved between them, V = W/Q; 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb. Here it is the voltage across the resistor's two ends.
nodes.plain_words: The push across its two ends is the voltage: two volts, two joules per coulomb.
nodes.what_is_lost: 'Push' is the story word; the proper meaning (energy per unit charge) is spoken and carded beside it. The cell's voltage equals the voltage across the resistor only for an ideal cell and wires (no internal resistance), which this circuit assumes.

nodes.statement: 1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second (12.1); 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb (12.2); 1 ohm = 1 volt per ampere (12.3).
The cell and wires are ideal: the whole cell voltage appears across the resistor's two ends.
nodes.what_is_lost: A real cell has internal resistance and the wires a little resistance, so the voltage across the resistor is slightly less than the cell's rating.

nodes.statement: For a conductor at constant temperature, the current through it is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.
The ratio V/I is constant for such a conductor; this constant is its resistance R, so V = I × R.
The potential difference, V, across the ends of a given metallic wire in an electric circuit is directly proportional to the current flowing through it, provided its temperature remains the same.
nodes.spoken_as: Ohm's law says that current grows in step with the push. That holds while the temperature stays the same.

nodes.statement: A bulb filament gets hot when current flows; a hot filament resists more (its resistance rises as it heats), so its V–I graph is not a straight line and doubling the voltage does not double the current.
nodes.reliability_note: NCERT states the constant-temperature condition (Ohm's Law) and describes the hot filament (Heating Effect); it does not state in one sentence that filament resistance rises with temperature. That is standard physics at this level but needs subject review. The claim stays qualitative: no lamp current number exists anywhere in this build (PD-16).

nodes.statement: Doubling the voltage always doubles the current.
nodes.why_wrong: Only while the resistance stays constant; a filament heats, its resistance rises, so the current rises by less than double.

nodes.statement: Voltage is described as the push that drives current, resistance as what holds it back, current as the flow the meter counts.
nodes.what_is_lost: Voltage is energy per unit charge; 'push' does not say how much energy each charge carries. Nothing is used up: the same current flows all round the loop.

nodes.statement: The resistor is treated as staying at exactly the same temperature at two and four volts.
nodes.what_is_lost: A real resistor warms slightly with current; the change is negligible here but not zero.

nodes.prompt: A ten-ohm resistor at two volts: calculate the meter reading; then double the voltage to four volts and predict it.
steps: 4 V ÷ 10 Ω = 0.40 A: the same resistance, so twice the voltage gives twice the current (ratio 2).
V ÷ I = 10 Ω at both points: the resistance did not change.

nodes.prompt: Same two volts, resistance doubled to twenty ohms: the current.
steps: Double R at the same V halves I (0.20 A → 0.10 A).

nodes.statement: Plotting V against I for the resistor gives a straight line through the origin; its slope V/I is the resistance R. Points (0, 0), (0.20 A, 2 V), (0.40 A, 4 V), (0.60 A, 6 V).
nodes.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, section 12.3, Activity 12.1 and its V–I graph for a nichrome wire (figure number to be confirmed against the current edition)

nodes.statement: The animated current dashes move round the loop at a speed proportional to the meter reading (2 V slow, 4 V twice as fast); at the resistor the flow narrows (it is held back); in the hot filament the dashes slow.
nodes.what_is_lost: Dash speed is not electron drift speed (drift is millimetres per second and the same current flows everywhere in the loop); the narrowing is a picture of opposition, not of a thinner current; the filament slowdown is qualitative only (no lamp current value exists, PD-16).
